title: Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Link Format
summary: This RFC defines a link format for constrained web servers to describe hosted resources and their attributes and relationships. It is based on the HTTP Link header, is carried as a payload with its own media type, and uses a well-known URI for discovery.

plainLanguage.summary: Small devices list what they offer, so a visitor can read the menu before ordering.

questions: how to discover resources on a coap server
what do rt and if mean in coap links
what is the sz attribute in link format
subtitle: A compact list format that lets tiny web servers tell clients what resources they host and how to use them.

tldr.problem: Machine-to-machine clients talking to constrained devices have no human to tell them which resources a server hosts, and fixed, hard-wired interfaces are fragile.
tldr.mechanism: Servers publish a list of links in a compact format based on the HTTP Link header, served at the well-known path /.well-known/core. Each link can carry attributes such as rt, if and sz, and clients can filter the list with a query string.
tldr.outcome: A client can GET one known URI and learn what a server offers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 6690 is a Proposed Standard from August 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the CoRE Link Format, the /.well-known/core entry point and the rt, if and sz attributes.

sections.title: Why Constrained Servers Need Discovery
sections.content:
The Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) work brings the REST architecture to very constrained nodes, such as 8-bit microcontrollers with limited memory, and to constrained networks such as 6LoWPANs. It targets machine-to-machine (M2M) uses like smart energy and building automation.

In these settings no human is in the loop and static interfaces are fragile, so clients must discover what a server hosts. RFC 6690 extends the HTTP Link header format from RFC 5988 into the CoRE Link Format. The links are carried as a payload, not as a header, and the format has its own Internet media type. It applies to CoAP, HTTP or any other suitable web transfer protocol.

The RFC sketches three use cases: unicast or multicast discovery of resources, finding and walking collections of resources, and a resource directory, which it likens to a limited search engine for constrained resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Little gadgets cannot be asked in person what they do. So each one writes a short list of its features that any other machine can read.

sections.title: The Link Format
sections.content:
A link is written as a target URI-reference in angle brackets, followed by semicolon-separated parameters. Several links are separated by commas, and commas inside quoted strings or URIs do not end a link. For example: </sensors/temp>;if="sensor". The format needs no XML or binary parsing, is fairly compact and is extensible. It is encoded as UTF-8, and decoders are not expected to validate or normalize it.

The RFC repeats the ABNF of RFC 5988 with improvements and new link parameters. The parameter name href is reserved for query filtering and MUST NOT be defined as a link parameter.

The default relation type is the new hosts: a link without a rel parameter means the server indicated by the context URI hosts the target resource, and the target MUST then be a relative URI. The context URI is the anchor parameter when given, otherwise the origin of the target URI, otherwise the origin of the link format resource's base URI. A consumer may choose to ignore anchored links.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line on the menu is a name in pointy brackets plus a few notes after semicolons. If a line says nothing else, it just means this gadget has that thing.

sections.title: The rt, if and sz Attributes
sections.content:
Three CoRE-specific target attributes are added. Each MUST NOT appear more than once in a link. When attribute values are compared, they MUST be compared as strings.

  • rt (Resource Type) is an opaque string giving a resource an application-specific semantic type, like a noun. Examples are outdoor-temperature or a URI pointing to an ontology concept. Several types may be separated by spaces. It is not a human-readable name; that is what title is for.
  • if (Interface Description) names or points to the interface definition used to interact with the resource, like the verbs usable on it. It is expected to be reused across Resource Types. Examples are a WADL URI, a URN such as urn:myapp:sensor or a plain name like sensor.
  • sz (Maximum Size Estimate) estimates the largest representation a GET on the target can return. For CoAP resources it is not expected for small resources that fit in one MTU, but SHOULD be included for larger ones. There is no upper limit, so implementations MUST accept large values and may map oversized ones to a special value such as "Big".
sections.plainLanguage: The notes say what a thing is (rt), how to talk to it (if) and roughly how big it is (sz), so you know if it will fit in your backpack.

sections.title: The Well-Known Interface and Filtering
sections.content:
Discovery uses the well-known path /.well-known/core, defined using the mechanism of RFC 5785. A server implementing the RFC MUST support this resource on the default port of the protocol. Its representation MUST be the CoRE Link Format, and with no links a zero-length payload is returned. The application decides which links are listed and how they are organized, for instance by linking to other link-format resources to build an index.

A GET returns the links. A server MAY treat the query string as a filter, matching the pattern /.well-known/core{?search*} from RFC 6570. The name is href, a link parameter or an extension name, and the value is either a complete value or a prefix followed by an asterisk. For example, ?foo=bar* matches any link with a foo attribute starting with bar, and ?foo=* matches any link that has foo. Matching is bitwise, and each value of a multi-valued attribute is matched separately.

Very constrained nodes are not expected to support filtering. A server without it MUST ignore the query and return the whole resource for unicast requests. For multicast requests, a server SHOULD NOT respond when it lacks filtering support or the filter does not match, to avoid a response storm. Resource directory functions, such as servers POSTing to /.well-known/core, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: You can shout your question at one gadget or a whole room. If you add a filter like "only lights", gadgets that are not lights stay quiet so the room does not explode with answers.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples use CoAP codes; with HTTP the response would be 200 OK. A plain GET on /.well-known/core can return </sensors/temp>;if="sensor",</sensors/light>;if="sensor", meaning the origin server hosts those two sensors, both sharing one Interface Description.

Links can also be arranged hierarchically: the entry point lists /sensors, and a GET on that returns the individual sensors with their rt and if values. Adding ?rt=light-lux returns only the light sensor. Because relation-type attributes can hold several space-separated values, that query also matches a link with rt="light-lux core.sen-light".

The anchor parameter can relate a resource to an external description, with rel="describedby" or rel="alternate", and a client can query by anchor. A firmware example carries sz=262144 so a client can decide whether block transfer is needed, and notes that a client with only a 64 KiB flash might store sz in 16 bits and use a special "Big" value.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask one gadget for its menu and you get a list. Ask for "only the light sensor" and you get just that one line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC inherits the security considerations of RFC 5988. The /.well-known/core resource MAY be protected, for example with DTLS when hosted on a CoAP server. Servers with authentication and authorization features SHOULD use the authentication of the underlying transport (HTTP or DTLS/TLS) and MAY return different link lists depending on who is asking.

Hiding a link is not access control: a bad actor could know or guess the right URI. Servers can also lie about what they host, so a client that needs a trusted source has to authenticate it.

Multicast CoAP requests to the well-known link-format resources could be used for denial of service on a constrained network. A multicast request SHOULD only be accepted if it is sufficiently authenticated and secured, for example with IPsec or an object security mechanism. Parsers must also expect cyclical links, direct or indirect, and take care when following them.
sections.plainLanguage: Not showing something on the menu does not lock the kitchen door. And a gadget might fib about its menu, so check who you are talking to.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the core well-known URI suffix, the hosts relation type and the media type application/link-format (file extension wlnk, encoding UTF-8).

It also creates a Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Parameters registry with two sub-registries, one for rt values and one for if values, with no initial entries. Values starting with core use IETF Review; all others use Specification Required, with review by a designated expert. Registered values MUST follow the reg-rel-type ABNF: a lowercase letter followed by lowercase letters, digits, periods or hyphens. URIs are reserved for free use as extension values and MUST NOT be registered. The expert approves or denies within at most 14 days.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official notebook where people write down the names they use for kinds of things, so two gadgets do not use the same name for different ideas.
